..
Issued at 240 AM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

A closed upper low was noted over NV per the 07Z water vapor 
imagery. Over the plains, southwest flow persisted between a broad 
upper ridge along the TX/LA gulf coasts. Surface obs placed a low 
over east central CO with a cold front extending east through the 
state. Better moisture return through the southern plains was also 
seen as middle 70s dewpoints were almost to the Red River. 

Continued moisture advection into the surface front across the 
forecast area should allow the boundary layer to become moderately 
unstable with MUCAPE values between 2000 and 3000 J/kg. On top of 
that stronger southwesterly upper flow over the boundary should 
increase bulk shear values to around 50KT. So there looks to be the 
potential for severe storms developing along the boundary late this 
afternoon. Most guidance shows low level flow veered to the 
southwest for much of the day. But towards 00Z the 850 winds are 
progged to back more to the south. This increased convergence along 
the boundary should be what helps convection to initiate and last 
into the early morning hours. The bulk shear will be supportive of 
supercell structure with the storms. So large hail and damaging 
winds will be a concern. The tornado risk still looks conditional on 
the local wind fields along of the boundary. 

Abnormally high moisture content is forecast ahead of the boundary 
with PWs around 2 inches. This would be a record value for 00Z/14 
and a couple standard deviations above the mean. So thunderstorms are 
expected to be efficient rainfall producers with rates around 2 
inches per hour realistic. Overall for the entire event through 
Thursday, blends and ensembles are showing increasing probabilities 
for exceeding 2 and 3 inches of rain across east central KS. With 
how unusually moist the airmass is, felt it prudent to go with a 
flood watch for east central KS. After collaboration the higher 
confidence in heavy rain was for tonight. So the watch has been 
posted into Wednesday morning. But if models continue to show 
another slug of moisture lifting into eastern KS with the upper wave 
Wednesday night and Thursday, the watch may need to be extended into 
the day Thursday. Other changes to the NBM was to lower high temps 
for today and Wednesday. For some reason the blend doesn't resolve 
the surface front very well and has temps in the lower and middle 
90s through the NEB state line. Based on the shorter term models 
keeping the boundary across the forecast area through the day, 
blended in some CONSRaw and CONSShort for highs today to show a 
stronger gradient in temps north to south. For Wednesday there is a 
good signal for stratus to setup over the area as north and 
northeast wind provide some weak cool air advection. But the limited 
insolation alone should be enough to hold temps in the 60s for 
Wednesday. 

The better synoptic scale forcing is forecast to impact the area 
late Wednesday night and Thursday as the upper low begins to phase 
in with the northern stream. Because of it phasing with the northern 
stream, we shouldn't see a negatively tilted wave lift over the 
forecast area. But there does look to be enough PVA for a surface 
wave to lift through eastern KS Thursday. A warm conveyor belt is 
progged to bring good moisture advection back into eastern KS. So 
have continued with the categorical POPs from the NBM. Eventually 
the wave should push east of the area Thursday evening. Strong 
northwest flow aloft is expected to help bring a Canadian surface 
high into the plains with some of the coolest temps so far this 
fall. A classic radiational setup for Saturday morning, with light 
winds and clear skies, could help temps drop into the middle 30s and 
allow for some frost to develop. The GFS and ECMWF show a low 
amplitude wave lifting across the forecast area Sunday night. So 
can't argue with the NBM's slight chance POPs inserted into the 
forecast. Although confidence in the smaller scale details typically 
isn't that high for day 6 and 7.
